title: Exploring LLM-Generated Feedback for Economics Essays: How Teaching Assistants Evaluate and Envision Its Use
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether LLM-generated feedback can serve as useful suggestions for human instructors when grading knowledge-intensive student writing, and how such feedback should be presented to support human review. Rather than testing student learning outcomes, the study focuses on teaching assistants’ experiences comparing AI-generated feedback with their own handwritten comments on economics essays.

The authors developed an LLM-based feedback pipeline for short essay responses in an introductory college economics course. The system decomposed feedback generation into modular steps: identifying relevant evidence in the essay, judging whether a rubric criterion was met, and generating a feedback comment. The feedback was visualized as in-text comments in a Word document, alongside highlighted sentences and, in some cases, retrieved historic instructor feedback. GPT-4o was used to generate the AI feedback.

The study was conducted in Fall 2024 in one university ECON101 course with 5 teaching assistants over 20 one-hour think-aloud sessions across four writing assignments. TAs first graded essays as usual, then reviewed AI feedback on the same essays and discussed whether they would use it in practice. The findings suggest that AI feedback was often more detailed, more rubric-aligned, and more likely to include praise, explanations, and guiding questions than human comments. TAs felt it could speed reading and comment writing, improve consistency, and act as a useful second opinion.

At the same time, participants noted important limitations: the system could be overly rigid, miss broader conceptual misunderstandings, and fail when rubrics were underspecified. The paper concludes that AI feedback is best treated as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for human judgment, and that explicit rubrics, sentence highlights, and intermediate outputs are important design features for useful human-AI collaboration.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, IRB-approved think-aloud study with 5 TAs and no randomized comparison or quantitative outcome estimation. It provides credible exploratory evidence about usability and perceived value, but not causal evidence of learning or productivity effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but subjective benefits such as faster grading and better feedback quality, without measured effect sizes or student outcomes. Impact appears modest and unclear at the population level because the evidence is based on a small, specialized sample and qualitative judgments.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated rubric-based feedback on college economics essays, presented as in-text comments with highlighted evidence and suggested revisions for teaching assistants to review and potentially reuse

finding.finding_summary: In think-aloud sessions with 5 teaching assistants over 20 one-hour sessions across 4 writing assignments, participants consistently reported that AI-generated feedback and sentence highlights would expedite grading and feedback writing. They described the system as saving time in reading, locating evidence, constructing comments, and standardizing decisions, but these were perceptions rather than measured productivity gains; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: TA perceptions of grading speed, time saved reading and writing feedback, and workflow efficiency from think-aloud interviews

finding.finding_summary: The AI feedback was perceived as more detailed, personalized, and aligned with rubric criteria than human/instructor historical feedback, often including praise, explanations, and guiding questions that TAs valued. However, participants also noted that rubric-driven feedback could be too rigid, overly fragmented, or miss broader writing quality and deeper conceptual issues, so the perceived quality advantages were conditional rather than uniform.
finding.measure: TA evaluations of feedback quality, specificity, personalization, and rubric alignment for economics essay comments
